claim: Growth firms are high-duration assets and value firms are low-duration assets, analogous to long-term versus short-term bonds, because growth firms' cash flows are weighted further into the future.
stance_target: Apple's rate sensitivity depends on where its cash flows are weighted in time (duration), not on 'growth stock' labeling alone
scope_conditions: Dynamic asset-pricing model calibrated to US aggregate stock market data
quoted_support: Analogous to long-term bonds, growth firms are high-duration assets while value firms are low-duration assets.
time_period: calibrated to historical US market data through early 2000s

claim: The model reproduces a value premium of 5.1% versus 4.9% observed empirically, and a CAPM alpha on the value-minus-growth strategy of 6.0% versus 5.6% empirically, while extreme value portfolios have LOWER standard deviation and market beta than extreme growth portfolios.
stance_target: value premium as compensation for discount-rate/duration risk rather than traditional risk measures
scope_conditions: Simulated data from calibrated model, portfolios formed by sorting on book-to-market
quoted_support: The value premium ... is 5.1% in the model compared with 4.9% in the data when portfolios are formed by sorting on book-to-market. Moreover, the CAPM alpha on the value-minus-growth strategy is 6.0% in the model, compared with 5.6% in the data.

claim: Empirically, growth stocks have measurably higher cash-flow duration than value stocks, and this duration difference contributes to growth stocks' higher betas (per Dechow, Sloan & Soliman 2004, cited by Lettau & Wachter).
stance_target: equity duration is empirically measurable and differs materially across growth/value
scope_conditions: US equities, cash-flow duration measured via Dechow-Sloan-Soliman methodology
quoted_support: Dechow, Sloan, and Soliman (2004) measure cash flow duration of value and growth portfolios; they find that empirically, growth stocks have higher duration than value stocks and that this contributes to their higher betas.

claim: Growth stocks have higher betas with respect to discount-rate news specifically (not just cash-flow news), consistent with the duration interpretation, per Campbell & Vuolteenaho (2004) cited by Lettau & Wachter.
stance_target: long-duration equities are measurably more sensitive to discount-rate shocks
scope_conditions: US equities, return decomposition into cash-flow news and discount-rate news
quoted_support: They show that growth stocks have higher betas with respect to discount rate news than do value stocks, consistent with the view that growth stocks are high-duration assets.

claim: Within the model, the sensitivity of an asset's price to a discount-rate shock is non-monotonic in the maturity of its cash flow claim: it becomes more negative up to roughly a 10-year maturity, then partially reverses because rising exposure to expected-dividend-growth news offsets the pure duration effect.
stance_target: a naive assumption that discount-rate sensitivity rises monotonically and without bound as cash-flow horizon lengthens
scope_conditions: model-internal decomposition of zero-coupon equity claims by maturity n
quoted_support: It is not surprising that (n) initially decreases in maturity. This is the duration effect... More curious is the fact that (n) rises after a maturity of 10 years. This is because the duration effect is countered by the increase in B(n).
